name: ATD (1,4,6-androstatrienedione)

lead: ATD is a steroid-like supplement ingredient sold over the counter in the prohormone era, reportedly until around 2009. Muscle-building circles discuss it for limiting estrogen conversion, aiming for less water retention and fewer gynecomastia concerns.

It is described as an irreversible aromatase inhibitor, binding the enzyme that makes estrogen from androgens and inactivating it. Support comes from enzyme studies and an old monkey study; no human trial of its effects on muscle, gynecomastia or appearance was found.

paras: It was sold as an oral supplement, usually alongside prohormones or steroids during a cycle. Products carried varied names.
No human safety data were found. It is banned in sport and can reportedly cause a positive boldenone test. Products under varied names can be hard to identify.

angle.text: ATD is a prohormone-era aromatase inhibitor used to limit conversion of androgens to estrogen, aiming for less water and fewer gynecomastia concerns. Lab data support the mechanism, and no human trial has tested the look-related claims.

lead: ATD (1,4,6-androstatriene-3,17-dione) is a steroid-type compound described as an irreversible aromatase inhibitor, meaning it binds the enzyme that converts androgens into estrogens and permanently inactivates it [1][2]. It was sold in over-the-counter bodybuilding and prohormone-era supplements, reportedly until around 2009, and is discussed in muscle-building circles as a way to limit estrogen conversion [2].

Laboratory work has examined ATD-related structures as aromatase inhibitors in human placental enzyme preparations [1]. No published human trial of ATD for body composition, gynecomastia or any other appearance outcome was identified. It is banned in sport as an aromatase inhibitor [2].
infobox: Oral; topical versions were also sold [2]
Former OTC supplement ingredient; banned in sport [2]

paras: ATD is described as binding aromatase and permanently inactivating it in fat and other peripheral tissue, which lowers estrogen production [2]. A 1981 study cited by Wikipedia described enzyme-generated intermediates that progressively reduce placental aromatase activity [2]. A 1995 chemistry paper evaluated 4-thio-substituted derivatives of 1,4,6-androstatrienedione and related dienediones and reported potent inhibition of aromatase in human placental microsomes [1].

ATD appeared in some over-the-counter supplements until 2009, and topical products were also marketed [2]. Wikipedia credits supplement-industry figure Bruce Kneller with developing and commercialising it and notes he holds a related US patent [2]. Sellers used many alternative names, which can make products harder to identify [2].

ATD is prohibited in amateur and professional sport as an aromatase inhibitor. It is also reported that ATD can produce a positive test for the anabolic steroid boldenone, of which it is a possible metabolite and manufacturing contaminant [2].

No studies found. A 1984 study in rhesus monkeys, cited by Wikipedia, reported that aromatase inhibition increased luteinizing hormone and testosterone secretion; this was animal research and not a test of appearance outcomes [2].

timeline.event: Study describes enzyme-generated intermediates of ATD that progressively reduce placental aromatase activity [2].
Rhesus monkey study reports raised LH and testosterone with aromatase inhibition [2].
Paper reports 4-thio derivatives of 1,4,6-androstatrienedione as potent aromatase inhibitors in vitro [1].
Approximate end of ATD's presence in over-the-counter supplements [2].
